conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that arthroscopy does not help osteoarthritis of the knee in a clinically meaningful way, citing strong evidence from trials and clinical guidelines recommending against its use.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion: No—arthroscopy generally does not help osteoarthritis (OA) of the knee in a clinically meaningful way.** For people with degenerative knee disease (OA, often with degenerative meniscal tears), the best evidence finds little or no important improvement in pain or physical function compared with placebo surgery or non-surgical care.

Why this conclusion is strong:

- A placebo-controlled randomized trial found that arthroscopic lavage or debridement produced outcomes **no better than placebo surgery** in knee OA. https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259  
- A later randomized trial in moderate-to-severe OA compared arthroscopy plus optimized medical/physical therapy against optimized therapy alone, testing whether surgery added value. https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0708333  
- The 2022 Cochrane systematic review concluded arthroscopy provides “little or no clinically important benefit” for pain or function, probably no important knee-specific quality-of-life benefit, and may not improve treatment success versus placebo. https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD014328_arthroscopic-surgery-degenerative-knee-disease  
- Accordingly, the BMJ Rapid Recommendations panel issued a **strong recommendation against arthroscopy in nearly all patients with degenerative knee disease**, including those with imaging evidence of OA, mechanical symptoms, or sudden symptom onset. https://www.bmj.com/content/357/bmj.j1982  

Arthroscopy also entails recovery burden and surgical risks. This evidence concerns OA/degenerative disease; it should not be assumed to answer whether arthroscopy is appropriate for a different problem, such as an acute traumatic injury requiring repair.
